newsitem.title: GERMANY: Row seen brewing within Daimler over revamp plans.
newsitem.headline: Row seen brewing within Daimler over revamp plans.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG on Friday appeared to be on a collision course with the management of its flagship automotive subsidiary Mercedes-Benz AG over a proposed management revamp.

Sources close to Germany's largest industrial group said the management of Mercedes, headed by chief executive Helmut Werner, opposed a reported plan by Daimler chief Juergen Schrempp to integrate Mercedes fully into Daimler.
A report in local newspaper "Stuttgarter Zeitung" said Werner, whose position would effectively be made redundant by the move, had threatened to resign if the plan went ahead.
There was no official comment from the companies, which issued a statement reiterating that the group was discussing a reorganisation to make its management structure more efficient.
"Insofar as the media link this with speculation about personnel, we do not comment on that as a rule," it said.
Sources close to Daimler had said on Thursday that Daimler was considering a plan under which Mercedes would be merged with the parent company.

The plan is seen as part of a drive by Daimler-Benz chief Juergen Schrempp to take Daimler back to its roots as a transportation group, reversing the move by his predecessor Edzard Reuter to create an integrated technology holding group.

Following the dissolution earlier this year of its loss-making AEG industrial division and the bankruptcy of the majority-held Fokker Dutch plane-maker unit, analysts said such a move would be viewed as a logical next step.

Sources close to Daimler believe that an internal "merger" of the Mercedes-Benz car- and truck-making unit, which now makes up around three-quarters of its group revenues, would also likely be accompanied by management changes.

But the sources believed that Schrempp would seek to avoid any potentially damaging power struggle with Werner and could be ready to offer him the position of deputy chairman in the reshuffled Daimler board.
Any integration of Mercedes-Benz was moreover seen as almost certainly to be accompanied by the appointment of at least three current Mercedes managers to the main board.
But Werner's bargaining position within the company is seen as weaker than Schrempp's in that, unlike Daimler veteran Schrempp, he is a relative newcomer to the group.
The sources said that Daimler's aerospace unit Dasa and its Debis information systems unit had not yet figured strongly in discussions over the restructuring.

Schrempp, a champion of the drive for "shareholder value" in Germany, is under great pressure to fulfil a promise to return to profitability in 1996 after the 5.7 billion marks loss made by the group in 1995.
He said in late September that the restructuring was designed to make the group more responsive and that he hoped the first steps could be taken before the end of this year.
Friday's speculation did not hurt Daimler's share price, which closed floor trade up 1.35 marks at 89.80.
